h1: How to read a Telning book together
lead: Ten minutes, a few crayons, and one question at a time.
intro: You read a Telning book by looking, not by reading words. Your child tells the story, you ask one question per page, your child chooses the ending, and then you take the story into real life. This page shows you how.
byline: By the Telning team of cognitive and behavioural scientists

before.h2: What do you need before you start?

items.t: Short and often works better than long and rare.
Markers can come through the paper. See the tip below.
You both see the page. Your child sees you listening.

items.h: Let your child hold the book
items.t: The child turns the pages and sets the pace.

steps.h2: What are the four TADA steps?
steps.lead: The short version. The why, and the science behind it, is on the TADA page.

list.name: Talk
list.t: Says what they see. You wait, then add one or two words.

list.name: Ask
list.t: One easy question. Then one about feelings or why.

list.name: Decide
list.t: Picks one of the two endings and says why. No wrong answer.

list.name: Act
list.t: "What would you do?" Try it in real life. Then draw the ending and send it to Pim.

questions.h2: Questions to ask when reading with your child
questions.lead: Start easy. Move to feelings and why. End with your child's own life.

qs: When did you feel like that?

questions.tip: After a question, count to five in your head. Most children answer in that time.

ages.h2: How does it change with age?

list.name: Toddler
list.t: Point and name things together. You do more of the talking. One picture, one word, and lots of repeating.

list.name: Preschool
list.t: Your child tells more of the story. Ask one feeling question per page. Let your child choose the ending and colour it.

list.name: Early school
list.t: Your child tells the whole story and explains the choice. Ask why and what if. The drawing page is theirs.

dos.h2: What helps, and what gets in the way?
do: Read the same book again. Children learn from repeats.
A few short sessions a week beat one long one.
Wait after a question. Silence is thinking.
Repeat your child's words and add one.
dont: Do not quiz. One question per page is enough.
Do not rush to the "right" ending. There is none.
Do not explain the picture first. Let your child look.

marker.t: Crayons and pencils work best. If you use markers, put a sheet of paper behind the page.

items.a: Telning books are made for children from 0 to 7. Each book shows its age range on the cover. At 0 to 3 you do most of the talking; at 5 to 7 your child tells the whole story.

items.q: Do I need to read any words?
items.a: No. The books have no words. You look at the pictures together and talk. It works in any language you speak at home.

items.q: My child only scribbles. Is that OK?
items.a: Yes. Scribbling is how young children draw. The picture stays clear under a scribble, and the talk is what matters.

items.q: What if my child picks the "wrong" ending?
items.a: There is no wrong ending. Ask why they chose it, and what the other ending would change. That talk is the point.
Crayons and colouring (coloring) pencils work best. If you use markers, put a sheet of paper behind the page so the ink does not come through.

next.text: Take a photo of the drawing page and send it to Pim. A story card and ideas for your next talk come back by email.
